desc:
You are given a binary tree with distinct node values and a list of queries. Each query is a triple [type, a, b]; the answer to query i goes to position i of the result.

  • [1, v, k]: the value of the k-th ancestor of the node with value v (k = 1 is its parent, k = 2 its grandparent, ...). If the node has fewer than k ancestors the answer is -1. For k = 0 the answer is v itself.
  • [2, a, b]: the value of the lowest common ancestor of the nodes holding a and b (a node is its own ancestor here).
  • [3, a, b]: the distance, in edges, between the nodes holding a and b.

How trees are given. There is no tree type here. A binary tree is passed as an integer array in level-order (top to bottom, left to right). A missing child is written as -1, and every real node value is non-negative. The children of a missing node are not listed, and trailing -1 entries are dropped, so a non-empty array never ends with -1. The empty tree is [].

For example, [1, 2, 3, -1, 4] describes the tree on the left: the root is 1 with children 2 and 3, node 2 has no left child and has 4 as its right child, and node 3 is a leaf.

    1
   / \
  2   3
   \
    4

For the tree below ([3, 5, 1, 6, 2, 0, 8, -1, -1, 7, 4]) and ops = [[1, 7, 2], [2, 6, 4], [3, 7, 8], [1, 3, 1]] the answer is [5, 5, 5, -1]: the grandparent of 7 is 5, LCA(6, 4) = 5, dist(7, 8) = 5, and the root has no parent.

        3
      /   \
     5     1
    / \   / \
   6   2 0   8
      / \
     7   4
constraints: All node values are distinct, so a value identifies exactly one node
The array follows the encoding above exactly (valid level-order, no trailing -1)
Every v, a, b in a query occurs in the tree
Each query has exactly three integers; type is 1, 2 or 3; for type 1, 0 ≤ k ≤ 2,000
hints: Answering each query by climbing parent by parent costs O(depth). On a chain of 2,000 nodes with 1,500 queries that is millions of steps, so look for a way to jump.
Each node has one parent, so the 2j-th ancestor of a node is the 2j-1-th ancestor of its 2j-1-th ancestor. Precompute up[j][node] for all j up to log2(n).

k-th ancestor: if k exceeds the depth the answer is -1; otherwise jump by every power of two present in the binary form of k. LCA: lift the deeper node by the depth difference, then from the highest j to the lowest jump both nodes whenever up[j] differs. Distance: depth[a] + depth[b] - 2 * depth[lca].
editorial: Use binary lifting. Compute parent and depth of every node (one pass over the level-order array, since parents come first), then fill up[0] = parent and up[j][x] = up[j-1][ up[j-1][x] ], with -1 meaning 'above the root'. There are about log2 n tables, built in O(n log n).

A k-th ancestor query first checks k > depth[v] (answer -1) and then jumps once for every set bit of k. For the LCA, lift the deeper node to the depth of the other one; if they coincide that node is the answer; otherwise for j from high to low jump both nodes while up[j][a] != up[j][b], and the common parent up[0][a] is the LCA. The distance follows from depths and the LCA. Each query costs O(log n), so the whole solution is O((n + q) log n).

For this size a plain climb also passes in many cases, but it degrades to O(n · q) on deep trees; the lifting tables are the technique worth knowing, and they work unchanged for trees with millions of nodes.
